title: A Redis-compatible database in Rust with JSON, time-series and SQL built in
summary: A Redis-compatible database server in Rust that runs commands on different keys in parallel and builds in JSON, time-series, Bloom filters, schemas and SQL queries.

seo.metaTitle: Redis-compatible in-memory database written in Rust

videoFull.transcript: DRAFT, correct after recording. This is a Redis-compatible database, written from scratch in Rust, with JSON, time-series, Bloom filters, schemas and SQL built in. Existing Redis clients just work. It speaks the Redis protocol over TCP, stays wire-compatible so redis-cli and redis-benchmark run unchanged, and uses every CPU core so commands on different keys run at the same time. The stock redis-cli sets and reads keys, expiries and a sorted-set leaderboard. Then the extras: a JSON order read back by path, temperature readings in a time series, a Bloom filter check, and a SQL query listing every key by type. A collaborative whiteboard runs on top, with strokes appearing live in a second window and stored as list entries. An order book matches trades on sorted sets and writes each trade to a time series. Under the hood, Tokio runs a task per connection, a hand-written parser reads the protocol including partial and batched requests, the keyspace is a sharded map, and writes go to an append-only file through a background channel. The project's single-machine benchmark reports non-pipelined INCR about 42 percent faster than Redis, and pipelined writes far slower. Built by the ByteHint team.

videoShort.transcript: DRAFT, correct after recording. A Redis-compatible database written from scratch in Rust. The stock redis-cli works against it. On top of the usual commands it builds in JSON with paths, time-series, Bloom filters and a SQL query over the whole keyspace. A live whiteboard runs on it, with strokes appearing in a second window as they are drawn. Inside, a sharded map lets commands on different keys run in parallel, and disk writes happen in the background. The project's own single-machine benchmark puts non-pipelined INCR about 42 percent ahead of Redis and reports where Redis still wins. Built by the ByteHint team.

children.text: Redis is the default in-memory store, but it executes commands on a single thread, and JSON, time-series and probabilistic types need separate modules. The goal was a wire-compatible alternative in Rust that uses every core and ships those types built in.

problemChallenges.title: Single-threaded execution
problemChallenges.description: Independent writes from many clients queue behind one thread, even when they touch different keys.

problemChallenges.title: Features spread across modules
problemChallenges.description: JSON, time-series and Bloom filters each need a separate module to install and operate.

problemChallenges.title: No type checking on stored values
problemChallenges.description: Bad data reaches the store unchecked unless every application validates it.

problemChallenges.title: Staying wire-compatible
problemChallenges.description: Existing clients and tools must work unchanged, so the server has to speak the protocol exactly, including pipelined and partial frames.

problemChallenges.title: Durability without slowing writes
problemChallenges.description: Logging every write to disk inside the request path would cap throughput at disk speed.

problemConsequence: Teams keep paying for single-thread limits and run several modules to get the data types they need.

children.text: Developers start one binary and point any Redis client at it. Familiar commands work as before, and the same connection can store JSON documents, time series and Bloom filters, validate values against schemas, and query the keyspace with SQL. Prometheus metrics, a slow log and hot-key tracking are built in.

Technically, Tokio runs a task per connection, a hand-written parser reads the Redis protocol, and every value lives in one sharded DashMap so commands on different keys do not contend. Write commands are sent through a bounded channel to a background append-only-file writer.

features.title: Redis wire compatibility
features.description: A hand-written RESP parser handles partial and pipelined frames, so redis-cli, redis-benchmark and standard client libraries work unchanged.

features.title: Native JSON with JSONPath
features.description: Set, get and update parts of JSON documents by path, including array appends and numeric increments.

features.title: Time-series and Bloom filters
features.description: Time series with retention, labels and range queries, and Bloom filters for membership checks, with no modules to install.

features.title: Typed schemas
features.description: Define a schema, and typed writes are rejected when the value does not match it.

features.title: SQL over the keyspace
features.description: Select, count and delete keys by name pattern, type, memory or TTL with a SQL statement.

features.title: Built-in observability
features.description: A Prometheus endpoint with 13 metric families, a health endpoint, a slow log for commands over 1 ms and hot-key tracking.

children.text: The architecture diagram shows clients connecting over TCP, the protocol parser and auth gate, the command router, the sharded keyspace, and the background tasks for expiry, eviction and the write log, with metrics on a separate HTTP port.

The command sequence follows one write from raw bytes to reply, including the hand-off to the write log. The whiteboard sequence shows a real-time app built on the database, and the data model and auth flow fill in the details.

diagrams.title: One write, end to end
diagrams.caption: A SET from bytes to reply: frame parsing, auth check, a write to one shard, the async log hand-off and per-command metrics.
diagrams.mermaidSource:
sequenceDiagram
  box rgb(165,216,255) Client
    participant C as Redis client
  end
  box rgb(208,191,255) Server
    participant T as Connection task
    participant R as Router
    participant W as AOF writer task
  end
  box rgb(195,250,232) Data
    participant M as DashMap
    participant F as appendonly.aof
  end

  C->>T: *3 $3 SET $4 user $4 Asha (RESP)
  T->>T: buffer bytes, parse frame
  alt incomplete frame
    T->>T: wait for more bytes
  end
  T->>T: authenticated? else NOAUTH
  T->>R: route SET
  R->>M: insert into key's shard (other shards free)
  R->>R: evict if over max_memory
  R-->>T: +OK
  T->>W: try_send(command) to channel
  T->>T: record count, time, slow log if over 1 ms
  T-->>C: +OK
  W->>F: buffered write, fsync per policy

diagrams.title: Authentication
diagrams.caption: Per-connection password auth: commands are refused until AUTH succeeds, with PING and QUIT exempt.
diagrams.mermaidSource:
sequenceDiagram
  box rgb(165,216,255) Client
    participant C as Redis client
  end
  box rgb(208,191,255) Server
    participant T as Connection task
  end

  Note over T: RIVETDB_PASSWORD set, so require_auth = true
  C->>T: GET user
  T-->>C: -NOAUTH Authentication required
  C->>T: PING
  T-->>C: +PONG (exempt: AUTH, PING, QUIT, COMMAND)
  C->>T: AUTH wrong
  T-->>C: -ERR invalid password
  C->>T: AUTH correct
  T->>T: mark this connection authenticated
  T-->>C: +OK
  C->>T: GET user
  T-->>C: value
  Note over C,T: auth state lives per connection, a new connection starts unauthenticated

keyDecisions.title: Sharded concurrent map instead of one thread
keyDecisions.chose: DashMap plus a Tokio task per connection
keyDecisions.alternative: The single-threaded, lock-free event loop Redis uses
keyDecisions.why: Commands on different keys run in parallel. The project's benchmark shows the gain on non-pipelined commands and the cost under heavy pipelining, where per-command locking dominates.

keyDecisions.title: Write log through a channel
keyDecisions.chose: A bounded channel feeding a background append-only-file writer with a 64 KB buffer
keyDecisions.alternative: Writing and syncing inside the command path
keyDecisions.why: A slow disk never blocks a client. The trade-off is written in the code: when the channel is full, entries are dropped in favour of speed.

keyDecisions.title: Speak the Redis protocol
keyDecisions.chose: A RESP2 parser instead of a custom protocol
keyDecisions.alternative: A new protocol with its own client library
keyDecisions.why: Every demo uses a stock Redis client, and benchmarking uses Redis's own tool, so there is nothing new for developers to install.

keyDecisions.title: Extra types built into one value enum
keyDecisions.chose: JSON, time-series, Bloom filters and schemas as variants of one value type
keyDecisions.why: One binary, one memory estimate per value, and one keyspace that the SQL query command can scan by type.

keyDecisions.title: Real-time fan-out in the app layer
keyDecisions.chose: Socket.IO broadcasting in the demo, with state stored in the database
keyDecisions.why: The server has no pub/sub or transactions yet, so the demo apps handle broadcasting and order serialisation themselves.

technicalHighlights.detail: The Redis wire protocol over TCP for data, with a hand-written parser that handles partial and pipelined frames, and HTTP for metrics and health.
The keyspace is striped across DashMap shards inside one process, so commands on different keys do not wait on each other. It does not partition data across nodes.
An in-process bounded channel decouples the request path from the append-only-file writer, with write, flush and shutdown messages.
Built-in Prometheus metrics with 13 families, a health endpoint, a slow log and hot-key tracking, available without an external agent.
Tests on Linux, Windows and macOS across stable and nightly toolchains, format and lint checks, coverage upload and a release build artifact.
78 tests pass: 32 library and 46 command tests. 7 integration tests run against a live server.
12.64 percent of lines, measured with tarpaulin. Coverage is strongest in schemas, Bloom filters and auth, and lowest in the newer command families.
Structured tracing logs with a configurable level filter.
Optional per-connection password auth. Commands are refused until AUTH succeeds, with PING, QUIT and COMMAND exempt.
A single-process server. Demo apps are separate small services that talk to it over TCP.
Multi-stage images with dependency caching for the server and the whiteboard demo.
Controls that support compliance work: optional password auth, schema validation at write time, TTLs and time-series retention, and memory caps with eviction.
